Call a nonzero unital complex \(C^*\)-algebra \(M\) a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor if its center is \(\mathbb C1\), every subset \(S\subseteq M\) has right annihilator
\[
\{x\in M:sx=0\text{ for every }s\in S\}=pM
\]
for some projection \(p=p^*=p^2\), and every \(v\in M\) satisfying \(v^*v=1\) also satisfies \(vv^*=1\).

A quasitrace on a unital \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\) is a map \(q:A\to\mathbb C\) that is complex-linear on each abelian \(C^*\)-subalgebra and satisfies
\[
q(x^*x)=q(xx^*)\geq0,\qquad q(h+ik)=q(h)+iq(k)
\]
for every \(x\in A\) and self-adjoint \(h,k\in A\). It is a \(2\)-quasitrace if there is a quasitrace \(q_2\) on the matrix algebra \(M_2(A)\) such that \(q_2(\operatorname{diag}(x,0))=q(x)\) for every \(x\in A\). It is normalized if \(q(1)=1\), and faithful if \(q(x^*x)=0\) implies \(x=0\).

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of all real numbers \(\eta>0\) for which there exist a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor \(M\), a faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace \(\tau\) on \(M\), and self-adjoint elements \(a_0,a_1,\ldots\in M\) satisfying
\[
0\leq a_n\leq a_{n+1}\leq1,
\qquad
\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta
\qquad(n=0,1,2,\ldots),
\]
such that \((a_n)\) has no least upper bound in \(M_{\mathrm{sa}}=\{x\in M:x=x^*\}\). Here \(x\leq y\) means that \(y-x\) is positive in the \(C^*\)-algebra order.

Determine \(\mathcal G\) exactly.

## Overall result

The team **did not prove \(\mathcal G=\varnothing\)**. They proved the tracial, commuting, and finite-dimensional cases, developed several useful reductions and auxiliary lemmas, and found counterexamples to proposed shortcuts. **Nothing they found contradicts the prescribed answer.** The unresolved case is a genuinely noncommuting sequence in a diffuse finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor with a possibly nonlinear quasitrace.

Python checked finite algebraic identities and matrix examples—not the missing infinite-dimensional theorem.

## Main proved reductions

Write
\[
b_n=a_{n+1}-a_n.
\]
Then
\[
b_n\ge0,\qquad \sum_{n<N}b_n=a_N-a_0\le1,\qquad \tau(b_n)=\eta.
\]
Thus a sufficient, stronger statement would be **quasitracial exhaustion**: bounded positive partial sums force \(\tau(b_n)\to0\). They did not prove it. In particular, one cannot telescope quasitrace values as though \(\tau\) were linear.

For \(0<\eta\le1\), spectral projections
\[
p_n=1_{(\eta/2,1]}(b_n)
\]
satisfy
\[
\tau(p_n)\ge\frac{\eta}{2-\eta}\ge\frac\eta2,
\qquad
\sum_{n<N}p_n\le\frac2\eta\,1.
\]
The first inequality follows from
\(b_n\le(\eta/2)(1-p_n)+p_n\); the second from
\(b_n\ge(\eta/2)p_n\).
This reduces exhaustion to excluding an infinite **projection Bessel family** with uniformly positive dimension. Projection-lattice finiteness alone did not supply that exclusion.

They also proved sign/contraction bounds for positive partial sums, including
\[
\left\|\sum_i\varepsilon_i b_i\right\|\le1
\quad(\varepsilon_i=\pm1).
\]
No usable quasitracial cotype estimate followed.

## Complete special cases

If \(\tau\) is a trace on a subalgebra containing the sequence, then
\[
N\eta=\tau(a_N-a_0)\le1,
\]
a contradiction for sufficiently large \(N\). This covers commuting sequences.

For \(M=M_d(\mathbb C)\), the quasitrace axioms imply unitary invariance; abelian additivity then gives \(\tau(p)=\operatorname{rank}(p)/d\). Spectral decomposition shows \(\tau=\operatorname{Tr}/d\), so the same argument excludes all type-I finite factors.

## Connection with monotone sequential completeness

A substantial contribution was **constant-gap interpolation preserving the entire upper-bound set**.

Starting from a bounded increasing positive sequence \(s_n\) with uniform quasitracial tail gaps, choose \(k_n\uparrow\infty\) and put
\[
a_{n+1}=(1-t_n)a_n+t_ns_{k_n},\qquad
t_n=\frac{\eta}{\tau(s_{k_n}-a_n)}\in[\eta,1].
\]
Positive homogeneity gives \(\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta\). Every upper bound of \(s_n\) bounds \(a_n\). Conversely, repeated convex interpolation toward any fixed \(s_j\), with residual coefficient at most \((1-\eta)^r\), shows every upper bound of \(a_n\) bounds \(s_j\). Thus lack of a supremum is preserved.

They also reconstructed bounded quasitrace-Cauchy gluing, **using standard finite-\(\mathrm{AW}^*\) continuous-dimension, polar-decomposition, and matrix-stability facts**: fast spectral cutoffs produce projections \(e_k\uparrow1\) on which suitable subsequence columns converge in norm. Compatible bounded columns glue through the join of their graph projections in \(M_2(M)\). A uniform graph-angle bound passes to that join by rank continuity, yielding a bounded graph operator in \(M\). Positivity and order pass to the limit.

Subject to that standard background, these arguments identify the requested assertion with **monotone sequential completeness of finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factors**. They proved the surrounding reduction, not that structural theorem. No reliable theorem statement or citation establishing the missing step was located.

## Other reusable auxiliary results

The final new lemma was independently checked analytically:

> If \(0\le a\le b\) in an \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-algebra and \(a\ne b\), then either \(\|b\|>\|a\|\), or some rational \(t>0\), with \(q_t=1_{(-\infty,t)}(a)\), satisfies  
> \[
> \|q_tbq_t\|>\|q_taq_t\|.
> \]

For the contrapositive, set \(c=b-a\). Equal compression norms imply
\(q_tcq_t\le(t-a)q_t\). For a state \(\psi\), the positive functional
\[
f\mapsto\psi(c^{1/2}f(a)c^{1/2})
\]
defines a scalar Riesz measure \(\mu\). Continuous regularizers yield
\[
\int_{s<t}(t-s)^{-1}\,d\mu(s)\le1
\]
for rational \(t\), hence all \(t>0\) by lower semicontinuity. Tonelli forces \(\mu=0\), and therefore \(c=0\). This avoids assuming states are normal on spectral projections. Its application to an \(\omega_1\)-chain stalled because the detecting projections change with the reference element.

Other proved ingredients include finite-spectrum positive directional derivatives via Kato block diagonalization and pinching; a pinching-support rank identity; weighted projection-join estimates; a uniformly invertible contraction-product estimate for Bessel projections; and quasitracial-ultraproduct constructions from standard dimension theory. None closes exhaustion.

## Failed routes and genuine obstructions

* Operator square superadditivity is false: for two explicit \(2\times2\) projections \(A,C\), \(\det(AC+CA)=-1/4\).
* Real rank zero and stable rank one do **not** imply hyponormal elements are normal. Weighted truncated shifts in \(\prod M_N/\bigoplus M_N\) give a nonnormal hyponormal element. Its defect is quasitrace-null, so this does not refute faithful-quasitrace rigidity.

* Dimension-only packing inequalities admit the scalar model \(d(C)=\max(0,1-1/C)\); extensive exact checks show those inequalities alone cannot finish.

\[
\boxed{\mathcal G\subseteq(0,\tfrac12]}

and that \(\mathcal G\) is downward closed. They constructed no witness for any positive \(\eta\), and did not exclude \(\eta=\tfrac12\). Nothing they established contradicts the prescribed answer.

### 1. Quasitrace monotonicity and the upper bound

The final argument derives the needed monotonicity directly from standard AW\(^*\) spectral projections and polar decomposition, without assuming additivity on noncommuting positive elements.

For \(0\le x\le y\), set
\[
p=1_{(t+\varepsilon,\infty)}(x),\qquad
r=1_{(t,\infty)}(y).
\]
Then \(p\wedge(1-r)=0\): compression to a nonzero common subprojection would give \(x\ge(t+\varepsilon)1\) and \(y\le t1\), contradicting \(x\le y\). The polar decomposition of \(rp\) therefore makes \(p\) Murray–von Neumann equivalent to a subprojection of \(r\). Quasitrace invariance under equivalence and additivity on orthogonal projections give
\[
\tau(p)\le\tau(r).
\]
Spectral-step approximation, or integration of spectral tails followed by \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), yields \(\tau(x)\le\tau(y)\).

Writing \(b_n=a_{n+1}-a_n\), the inequalities
\[
b_{n-1}\le a_n,\qquad b_n\le1-a_n
\]
give, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
\eta\le\tau(a_n)\le1-\eta.
\]
Here \(\tau(1-a_n)=1-\tau(a_n)\) uses only linearity in the abelian algebra generated by \(a_n,1\). Thus \(\eta\le\tfrac12\). At equality, necessarily \(\tau(a_n)=\tfrac12\) for every \(n\ge1\).

### 2. Downward closure

If a sequence witnesses \(\eta_0\), then for \(0<\eta\le\eta_0\),
\[
c_n=(\eta/\eta_0)a_n
\]
witnesses \(\eta\). Homogeneity gives the required increments, and a least upper bound for \((c_n)\) would scale back to one for \((a_n)\).

Consequently, \(\mathcal G\) is either empty or an initial positive interval, with supremum at most \(\tfrac12\). This proves neither nonemptiness nor the location or inclusion of its endpoint.

### 3. Every witness requires a nontracial quasitrace

This is the central obstruction they identified. If \(\tau\) were additive on positive elements, then
\[
N\eta=\tau(a_N)-\tau(a_0)\le1,
\]
impossible for \(N>1/\eta\). Equivalently, positive additivity applied to
\[
1=a_0+\sum_{n<N}b_n+(1-a_N)
\]
would give \(1\ge N\eta\).

More quantitatively, defining
\[
D_n=\tau(a_{n+1})-\tau(a_n)-\eta,
\]
one has
\[
\sum_{n<N}D_n=\tau(a_N)-\tau(a_0)-N\eta\le1-N\eta.
\]
Since \(t_n=\tau(a_n)\) is increasing and bounded, \(t_{n+1}-t_n\to0\), so \(D_n\to-\eta\). A witness requires persistent negative additivity defects.

They also explained why finite von Neumann factors cannot supply examples. On matrix algebras, equivalence of rank-one projections and spectral decomposition force every normalized quasitrace to be normalized trace. In a type \(\mathrm{II}_1\) von Neumann factor, projection equivalence and comparison with rational-dimension projections determine quasitrace values on projections; spectral approximation then determines it on self-adjoint elements. Thus a witness would be a non-von-Neumann finite AW\(^*\)-factor, necessarily type \(\mathrm{II}_1\), and would contradict Kaplansky’s AW\(^*\)-factor conjecture. This is an implication, **not a contradiction of the problem’s asserted answer**.

For \(0<\delta<\eta\), spectral projections
\[
p_n=1_{(\delta,\infty)}(b_n)
\]

\sum_{n<N}p_n\le\delta^{-1}1,\qquad
\tau(p_n)\ge\frac{\eta-\delta}{1-\delta}>0.
\]
Thus a witness would produce infinitely many uniformly positive-quasitrace projections with bounded partial sums. They did not rule this out or construct it.

They investigated
\[
K=\sup\left\{\sum_i\tau(c_i):c_i\ge0,\ \sum_i c_i\le1\right\}.
\]
For finite \(K\), they gave a compactness/separation proof of a dominating state \(\phi\) with \(\tau(c)\le K\phi(c)\) for all \(c\ge0\). Their proposed continuation—using GNS strong* approximation and quasitracial metric completion to deduce that \(\tau\) is a trace—remained dependent on completion and continuity machinery not fully verified in the record. It should not be treated as a self-contained proved theorem here. Even \(K=\infty\) would still need a uniformization/construction argument.

* **Existence:** no example for even one positive \(\eta\), hence no verification of the no-least-upper-bound requirement.
* **Endpoint:** faithfulness gives \(\tau(d)>0\) for nonzero positive \(d\), but does not by itself justify \(\tau(a+d)>\tau(a)\). They found no valid strict-monotonicity argument.

  b=\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.

### 1. Upper bound: two increments suffice

Write \(d_n=a_{n+1}-a_n\). Then
\[
0\le d_0\le a_1,\qquad 0\le d_1\le1-a_1.
\]
Using order preservation of the quasitrace,
\[
\eta\le\tau(a_1),\qquad
\eta\le\tau(1-a_1)=1-\tau(a_1).
\]
The equality uses linearity on the abelian algebra generated by \(a_1\) and \(1\). Adding gives \(2\eta\le1\).

Thus the upper bound needs only two increments, not the infinite sequence or the absence of a least upper bound.

**Justification of order preservation.** Agent 3 supplied an AW*-spectral proof, using standard consequences of the AW* axiom: spectral projections, projection meets, and polar decomposition.

For \(x\ge0\), let
\[
e_t(x)=\operatorname{supp}((x-t)_+).
\]
If \(0\le a\le b\), \(t\ge0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), set
\[
e=e_{t+\varepsilon}(a),\qquad f=e_t(b).
\]
Then \(e\wedge(1-f)=0\). Indeed, a common nonzero subprojection \(r\) would satisfy
\[
rar\ge(t+\varepsilon)r,\qquad rbr\le tr,
\]
contradicting \(rar\le rbr\).

The polar decomposition of \(fe\) consequently has initial projection \(e\) and final projection \(g\le f\). Hence
\[
\tau(e)=\tau(g)\le\tau(f).
\]
Here the equality follows from the quasitrace identity for \(v^*v,vv^*\), and the inequality follows from additivity on the commuting orthogonal projections \(g,f-g\).

Spectral step approximations within abelian subalgebras give
\[
\tau(x)=\int_0^{\|x\|}\tau(e_t(x))\,dt.
\]
Integrating the shifted spectral inequality yields
\(\tau(a)\le\tau(b)+\varepsilon\tau(1)\), and letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves monotonicity. This is a mathematical argument using AW* structure, not something verified by the Python calculations.

### 2. Downward closure

If \((M,\tau,(a_n))\) witnesses \(\eta\), and \(0<\eta'\le\eta\), put
\[
t=\eta'/\eta,\qquad a_n'=ta_n.
\]
These elements satisfy the order bounds, and abelian homogeneity gives
\[
\tau(a_{n+1}'-a_n')=t\eta=\eta'.
\]
If \(b\) were a least upper bound for \((a_n')\), then \(b/t\) would be a least upper bound for \((a_n)\), a contradiction.

Thus any nonempty \(\mathcal G\) is an initial interval. In particular, a witness at \(\eta=\tfrac12\) would establish the entire proposed lower inclusion.

### 3. Every witness forces genuine quasitrace nonadditivity

This is the principal obstruction identified by the team.

Choose an integer \(N\) with \(N\eta>1\), and set
\[
b_n=a_{n+1}-a_n\quad(0\le n<N).
\]
Then
\[
0\le s:=\sum_{n<N}b_n=a_N-a_0\le1.
\]
Linearity on \(C^*(s,1)\) alone implies \(0\le\tau(s)\le1\), whereas
\[
\sum_{n<N}\tau(b_n)=N\eta>1.
\]
Therefore \(\tau\) cannot be additive on positive elements. This argument does not require quasitrace monotonicity or the no-least-upper-bound hypothesis.

Consequences:

- No linear trace can support such a sequence: trace telescoping would give \(N\eta\le1\) for every \(N\).
- No commuting sequence can work, since its generated abelian algebra is a domain of linearity for \(\tau\).
- No von Neumann algebra can supply the required no-least-upper-bound sequence, because von Neumann algebras are monotone complete.
- Constructing even one witness would therefore produce a non-von-Neumann finite AW*-factor with a nonadditive faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace.

The team recognized this as a Kaplansky-type finite-AW*-factor/quasitrace obstruction, not a routine missing construction. They did **not** prove a converse: a hypothetical nonlinear quasitrace was not shown to yield the required sequence.

The entire existence direction remains open in this record: no factor, quasitrace, sequence, or external theorem supplying a witness was obtained.

- **Faithfulness does not immediately imply strict order preservation.** At \(\eta=\tfrac12\), the upper-bound argument forces \(\tau(a_n)=\tfrac12\) for \(n\ge1\). The team could not legitimately turn that into \(a_n=a_{n+1}\).
- **Projection completeness is not automatically arbitrary monotone completeness.** They did not establish that the AW* assumptions rule out the required no-lub sequence.
- Equal spectral distributions were not shown to imply exact unitary conjugacy or equality of ordered elements.
- Isometry-finiteness was not shown to imply that every hyponormal element is normal.
- No suitable uniform superadditivity estimate for quasitraces was proved. Familiar upper quasi-triangle estimates do not supply the needed lower estimate.
- Matrix diagonal pinching cannot simply be assumed quasitrace-preserving; that would import missing additivity.

\mathcal G=\varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{every finite }\mathrm{AW}^*\text{-factor is monotone sequentially complete}.
\;}
\]
Here monotone sequential completeness means that every norm-bounded increasing sequence of self-adjoint elements has a least upper bound. Thus proving the originally claimed answer would settle an existing open structural problem.

The nontrivial implication requires two ingredients: **bounded quasitracial completeness** and **constant-gap interpolation preserving upper bounds**. I give the details below.

## 1. Classical projection-theoretic ingredients

The following are standard consequences of finite-\(\mathrm{AW}^*\) dimension theory, not assertions of monotone completeness:

* A finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor has a canonical faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace.
* Its projection dimension is \(D(p)=\tau(p)\). It is faithful and continuous on increasing joins of projections:
  \[
  p_n\uparrow p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D(p_n)\uparrow D(p).
  \]
* \(M_2(M)\) is again a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor, with its compatible dimension function.
* Polar decomposition is available. Writing
  \[
  \rho(x)=D(\operatorname{supp}|x|),
  \]
  one has
  \[
  \rho(x+y)\le \rho(x)+\rho(y),\qquad
  \rho(xy)\le\min\{\rho(x),\rho(y)\}.
  \]
* The quasitrace is order preserving on positive elements.

The last fact does not assert additivity. It follows by comparing dimensions of shifted spectral projections and then integrating spectral tails.

## 2. Bounded quasitracial completeness

We need the following result.

**Lemma.** If \((x_n)\subset M\) is norm-bounded and
\[
\tau\!\left((x_n-x_m)^*(x_n-x_m)\right)\longrightarrow0
\qquad(n,m\to\infty),
\]
then there is \(x\in M\), with the same norm bound, such that
\[
\tau\!\left((x_n-x)^*(x_n-x)\right)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Moreover, self-adjointness and positivity pass to such bounded limits.

Here is a proof that uses projection completeness, rather than the unresolved order-completeness assertion.

### Bounded gluing on increasing projections

First suppose \(e_k\uparrow1\) are projections and \(y_k\in M\) satisfy
\[
y_ke_k=y_k,\qquad y_\ell e_k=y_k\quad(\ell\ge k),
\qquad \|y_k\|\le C.
\]
We claim that there exists \(x\in M\), \(\|x\|\le C\), with \(xe_k=y_k\).

Let \(r_k\in M_2(M)\) be the graph projection of the column
\[
\begin{pmatrix}e_k\\y_k\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compatibility implies \(r_k\le r_{k+1}\). Put
\[
r=\bigvee_k r_k,\qquad h=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad c=(1+C^2)^{-1}.
\]
The graph norm bound gives
\[
r_khr_k\ge c\,r_k.
\]
Also \(r_k\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{diag}(e_k,0)\), so projection-dimension continuity gives
\[
D_2(r)=\lim_kD_2(r_k)=\tfrac12.
\]

We may pass the graph-angle inequality to \(r\) without assuming monotone completeness. Indeed,
\[
\rho_2\!\left((rhr-cr)-(r_khr_k-cr_k)\right)
 \le 2D_2(r-r_k)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Positivity is closed under this rank convergence: if \(z_k\ge0\), \(z=z^*\), and \(\rho(z-z_k)\to0\), then any spectral projection of \(z\) below \(-\varepsilon\) has dimension at most \(\rho(z-z_k)\), and hence is zero. Consequently,
\[
rhr\ge cr.
\]

Thus \(hr\) is bounded below on its initial corner \(r\). Its range projection \(f\) satisfies
\[
f\le h,\qquad D_2(f)=D_2(r)=D_2(h),
\]
so faithfulness gives \(f=h\). Therefore \(r\) is the graph of a bounded \(x\in M\). The graph-angle bound gives \(\|x\|\le C\), and \(r_k\le r\) gives \(xe_k=y_k\). This proves the gluing claim.

### Constructing the quasitracial limit

Pass to a subsequence, denoted \(z_j\), such that
\[
\tau\!\left(|z_{j+1}-z_j|^2\right)\le2^{-4j}.
\]
Set
\[
p_j=1_{(2^{-j},\infty)}(|z_{j+1}-z_j|).
\]
Spectral calculus within an abelian subalgebra gives
\[
D(p_j)\le2^{-2j}.
\]
Define
\[
e_k=\bigwedge_{j\ge k}(1-p_j).
\]
Then
\[
D(1-e_k)\le\sum_{j\ge k}2^{-2j}\longrightarrow0,
\qquad e_k\uparrow1.
\]
For \(j\ge k\),
\[
\|(z_{j+1}-z_j)e_k\|\le2^{-j}.
\]
Hence \(z_je_k\) converges in norm to some \(y_k\), and these \(y_k\) satisfy the bounded gluing conditions. Obtain \(x\in M\) with \(xe_k=y_k\).

To verify convergence, use the elementary spectral estimate
\[
\tau(|z|^2)
 \le t^2+\|z\|^2D\!\left(1_{(t,\infty)}(|z|)\right).
\]
If \(\|ze\|<t\), then
\[
1_{(t,\infty)}(|z|)\wedge e=0,
\]
so the spectral projection in this estimate has dimension at most \(D(1-e)\). Applying this to \(z=z_j-x\) and \(e=e_k\) proves
\[
\tau(|z_j-x|^2)\longrightarrow0.
\]

These same “small in norm on a large projection” estimates show that sums preserve convergence. Thus the original Cauchy sequence, not merely the subsequence, converges to \(x\). Adjoint continuity follows from
\[
\tau(z^*z)=\tau(zz^*).
\]

Finally, positivity is closed. If \(x_n\ge0\), \(x=x^*\), and \(x_n\to x\) quasitracially, let
\[
p=1_{(-\infty,-\varepsilon)}(x),\qquad
e_n=1_{[0,\varepsilon/2]}(|x_n-x|).
\]
Compression shows \(p\wedge e_n=0\), whereas
\[
D(1-e_n)\le \frac4{\varepsilon^2}\tau(|x_n-x|^2)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore \(D(p)=0\), so \(p=0\), proving \(x\ge0\). This completes the lemma.

In particular:

> A bounded increasing quasitracially Cauchy sequence has a least upper bound.

Indeed, if its limit is \(x\), closedness of positivity gives \(s_n\le x\) for every \(n\). For any upper bound \(u\), it also gives \(x\le u\).

## 3. Failure of sequential completeness gives uniform tail gaps

Suppose a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor has a bounded increasing self-adjoint sequence without a least upper bound. An affine rescaling gives such a sequence satisfying
\[
0\le s_n\le s_{n+1}\le1.
\]

By the preceding lemma, \((s_n)\) cannot be quasitracially Cauchy. Therefore there is \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(k\), some \(m>k\) satisfies
\[
\tau(s_m-s_k)\ge\delta. \tag{1}
\]
To see this, non-Cauchyness first produces uniformly positive values of
\(\tau((s_m-s_n)^2)\). Since \(0\le s_m-s_n\le1\),
\[
\tau(s_m-s_n)\ge\tau((s_m-s_n)^2).
\]
Order preservation then allows replacement of \(n\ge k\) by \(k\).

## 4. Constant-gap interpolation preserves every upper bound

Fix \(0<\eta<\delta\), and put \(a_0=s_0\). Recursively choose strictly increasing indices \(k_n\), with \(k_n\ge n\), such that
\[
s_{k_n}\ge a_n,\qquad
\tau(s_{k_n}-a_n)\ge\delta.
\]
This is possible by (1), since the construction maintains
\(a_n\le s_{k_{n-1}}\).

Set
\[
t_n=\frac{\eta}{\tau(s_{k_n}-a_n)},\qquad
a_{n+1}=(1-t_n)a_n+t_ns_{k_n}.
\]
Because \(0\le s_{k_n}-a_n\le1\),
\[
\eta\le t_n\le\frac{\eta}{\delta}<1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
0\le a_n\le a_{n+1}\le1,
\qquad
\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta.
\]
The equality uses only positive homogeneity of the quasitrace.

Crucially, **the two sequences have exactly the same upper bounds**.

Every upper bound of \((s_n)\) bounds \((a_n)\), by convexity. Conversely, suppose \(u\ge a_n\) for all \(n\), and fix \(j\). For sufficiently large \(N\), \(k_n\ge j\) whenever \(n\ge N\), so
\[
a_{n+1}\ge(1-t_n)a_n+t_ns_j.
\]
Iteration gives
\[
a_{N+r}\ge P_ra_N+(1-P_r)s_j,
\qquad
P_r=\prod_{n=N}^{N+r-1}(1-t_n)
 \le(1-\eta)^r.
\]
Since \(P_r\to0\), norm-closedness of the positive cone yields \(u\ge s_j\).

Thus \((a_n)\) cannot have a least upper bound: such an element would also be a least upper bound of \((s_n)\). We have constructed a witness to \(\eta\in\mathcal G\).

## 5. The resulting equivalence

If every finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor is monotone sequentially complete, the no-least-upper-bound condition immediately rules out every witness.

Conversely, if any finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor fails monotone sequential completeness, Sections 2–4 produce a witness for some positive \(\eta\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\;
\mathcal G=\varnothing
\iff
\text{all finite }\mathrm{AW}^*\text{-factors are monotone sequentially complete}.
\;}
\]

One also has the unconditional restrictions
\[
\mathcal G\subseteq(0,\tfrac12],
\qquad
\mathcal G\ \text{is downward closed}.
\]
But these do not determine it exactly. In particular, neither emptiness nor any of the proposed nonempty intervals is currently established.
